messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo transducer (sinusoidal current source, Cp = 25 nF, 20 MOhm leak).
    *   Output node `out` feeds load RL (variable).
    *   Goal:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V
        *   $T_{up} \le 0.4$ s
        *   $dV \le 0.02$ V
    *   Operating conditions S1-S6 (varying load, excitation, and Cp/temp).
    *   Reference FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed:
        *   S2 (Heavy load): $V_{avg}$ too low.
        *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): $V_{max}$ too high, $V_{pp}$ too high.
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): $V_{avg}$ too low, $T_{up}$ missing.
        *   S5 (Low freq): $dV$ failing (stability).

    *   $V_{OC} \approx 3.2$ V. This is quite low. Diode drops in a full bridge (2 * 0.25V = 0.5V) are significant.
    *   The low $V_{OC}$ suggests that passive rectification (FBR) might struggle with efficiency (S2, S4).
    *   S3 (Light load, high excitation) causes $V_{out}$ to overshoot 3.6 V. A zener clamp or a voltage regulator is needed.
    *   The ripple requirement ($V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V) is quite strict. This requires a large storage capacitor $C_{out}$.
    *   Startup time ($T_{up} \le 0.4$ s) limits how large $C_{out}$ can be, as it needs to charge up from 0 V.

    *   *Topology 1: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)*.
        SSHI can significantly improve the voltage harvested by inverting the capacitor voltage at the peaks. This helps with $V_{avg}$ and $T_{up}$.
        Basic SSHI structure: Piezo $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Switch $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        Actually, the "Standard SSHI" is Piezo in parallel with an L-S flip circuit, followed by a rectifier.

    *   *Topology 2: Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE)*.
        SECE uses an inductor and a switch to extract charge when the piezo voltage reaches a peak.

    *   *Topology 3: Full Bridge Rectifier + Zener Clamp*.
        Since S3 failed on $V_{max}$, adding a Zener diode (DZ33) to the output is a simple fix for overvoltage. But this doesn't fix the low $V_{avg}$ for S2/S4.

    *   *Topology 4: SSHI (Simplified)*.
        L-S inversion circuit (Piezo $\to$ L $\to$ S) followed by a diode to $C_{out}$.
        Wait, the standard "Parallel SSHI" uses an L and a switch in parallel with the piezo to flip the voltage, then a diode to charge $C_{out}$.
        Let's try:
        - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
        - Inversion: L between pzp and n1, S between n1 and pzn.
        - Rectification: D from pzp to out.
        - Storage: C from out to 0.
        - Clamp: DZ33 from out to 0.

    *   *Topology 5: SECE-like structure*.
        Piezo $\to$ S $\to$ L $\to$ D $\to$ $C_{out}$.

    *   *Proposal 1: SSHI with Zener Clamp*.
        This targets the efficiency (S2, S4) via voltage inversion and the overvoltage (S3) via the Zener.
        Components:
        - L1: pzp to n1
        - S1: n1 to pzn (ctrl: G1)
        - G1: SYNC (edges: both, ton: pi*sqrt(L*Cp))
        - D1: pzp to out (DSCH)
        - C1: out to 0
        - D_clamp: out to 0 (DZ33)
        Wait, a single diode D1 only harvests half cycles. For better efficiency, a bridge or a half-wave with a different arrangement is needed. But if the inversion is perfect, the voltage is always pushed positive relative to pzn? No, the inversion happens at the peaks.
        Actually, the standard "Parallel SSHI" has the L-S branch across the piezo and a half-wave rectifier (D1) from the piezo to the storage. Since the polarity is flipped, D1 can conduct more often.

    *   *Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge)*.
        Replacing diodes with switches. But we only have 4 switches.
        An active bridge would use 4 switches.
        S1: pzp to out
        S2: pzn to out
        S3: 0 to pzp
        S4: 0 to pzn
        But we need separate controllers for the two phases. We have at most 2 SYNC.
        G1: edges: pos, S1 and S4.
        G2: edges: neg, S2 and S3.
        This removes the 0.5V drop, helping S2 and S4.

    *   *Proposal 3: SSHI with Full Bridge*.
        L-S flip + Full Bridge Rectifier + Zener Clamp.
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (G1)
        D1: pzp to out, D2: pzn to out, D3: 0 to pzp, D4: 0 to pzn.
        C1: out to 0.
        DZ1: out to 0.

    *   S3 failed on $V_{max} > 3.6$ V.
    *   S2, S4 failed on $V_{avg} < 1.8$ V.
    *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V is very tight.

    Let's refine Proposal 1 (Parallel SSHI):
    - L1: pzp $\to$ n1
    - S1: n1 $\to$ pzn (G1, both edges)
    - D1: pzp $\to$ out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn $\to$ out (Wait, pzn is the reference? No, pzn is the other piezo terminal. FBR is better).
    Actually, a full bridge is safer.

    Wait, looking at the "Reference Design" results:
    S2 $V_{avg} = 1.76$ (Close to 1.8)
    S4 $V_{avg} = 1.51$ (Further)
    The voltage drop is the main issue. SSHI increases the available voltage.

    Let's try:
    1.  **SSHI + FBR + Zener**: (L-S flip, Full Bridge, C-out, Zener)
    2.  **Active Rectification (Synchronous Bridge)**: (4 Switches, C-out, Zener)
    3.  **SSHI + Half-wave Rectifier + Zener**: (L-S flip, 1 Diode, C-out, Zener) - simpler, fewer components.

    Wait, if I use an active bridge, the switches close at the extrema? No, they should be closed for the whole half-cycle. But the `SYNC` controller only closes for `ton` (max 1ms). So `SYNC` is for *switching* (like in SSHI), not for *rectifying* (which requires half-cycle conduction).
    Therefore, the `S` components are intended for L-C inversion (SSHI/SECE), not for replacing diodes in a bridge.

    So, I will focus on SSHI and SECE.

    **Design A: SSHI + FBR + Zener**
    - L1: pzp to n1
    - S1: n1 to pzn (G1: edges=both, ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp))
    - D1: pzp to out, D2: pzn to out, D3: 0 to pzp, D4: 0 to pzn (DSCH)
    - C1: out to 0
    - D_clamp: out to 0 (DZ33)
    - *Problem*: 11 components.

    **Design B: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
    - S1: pzp to n1 (G1: edges=both)
    - L1: n1 to out
    - D1: n1 to out (Wait, SECE usually is Piezo $\to$ S $\to$ L $\to$ D $\to$ C)
    Let's refine:
    - S1: pzp to n1 (G1: edges=both, ton=small)
    - L1: n1 to n2
    - D1: n2 to out (DSCH)
    - C1: out to 0
    - D_clamp: out to 0 (DZ33)
    (Actually, a simpler SECE: S1: pzp to n1, L1: n1 to out, D1: n1 to out? No.)
    Standard SECE: S1: pzp to n1, L1: n1 to out. When S1 closes, charge flows through L1 to C1. But we need a diode to prevent reverse flow.
    Correct SECE: S1: pzp to n1, L1: n1 to n2, D1: n2 to out, C1: out to 0.
    Actually, a simpler version is just the SSHI.

    **Design C: SSHI + Half-wave Rectifier + Zener**
    - L1: pzp to n1
    - S1: n1 to pzn (G1: edges=both)
    - D1: pzp to out (DSCH)
    - C1: out to 0
    - D_clamp: out to 0 (DZ33)
    (This is a very common SSHI implementation).

    Let's re-evaluate the components for SSHI+FBR+Zener.
    L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, C1, D_clamp = 9 components.
    Wait, does the full bridge make sense with SSHI?
    In SSHI, the inversion flips $V_{pzp}$ to $-V_{pzp}$. If we have a full bridge, we harvest both polarities regardless of the flip. The flip just increases the voltage magnitude.

    Let's refine the "SSHI + Half-wave" (Design C). If we flip the voltage, the piezo voltage becomes mostly positive (or negative), so a single diode can harvest almost all the energy. This is more efficient (one diode drop instead of two).

    Let's try these three:
    1. SSHI + Half-wave (D1: pzp $\to$ out) + Zener.
    2. SSHI + Full-bridge (D1-D4) + Zener.
    3. SECE (S1: pzp $\to$ n1, L1: n1 $\to$ n2, D1: n2 $\to$ out) + Zener.

    Wait, for the Half-wave SSHI, the diode should be from `pzp` to `out` and the flip should happen at the peaks. If the switch flips the voltage at the positive peak, $V_{pzp}$ becomes negative. If it flips at the negative peak, $V_{pzp}$ becomes positive.
    If we want to use a diode from `pzp` to `out`, we want $V_{pzp}$ to be positive. So we should flip at the *negative* peak? No, the standard SSHI flips at both.

    Let's double check SSHI:
    At $t=t_{peak}$, the capacitor $C_p$ is charged. The switch closes, and $L$ and $C_p$ exchange energy, flipping the voltage. This happens at both extrema.
    Result: $V_{pzp}$ is shifted. The average voltage $V_{pzp}$ is no longer zero. A half-wave rectifier can then extract this DC component.

    Wait, looking at the Reference Design (FBR), $V_{avg}$ for S4 was 1.51V. To get to 1.8V, we need a $\sim 20\%$ increase. SSHI can easily provide this.

    Refining Proposal 1 (Half-Wave SSHI):
    - L1: pzp, n1
    - S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: edges: both, ton: 3e-5, phase: 0
    - D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    - C1: out, 0
    - D_clamp: out, 0 (DZ33)

    Refining Proposal 2 (Full-Bridge SSHI):
    - L1: pzp, n1
    - S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: edges: both, ton: 3e-5, phase: 0
    - D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
    - D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
    - D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
    - C1: out, 0
    - D_clamp: out, 0 (DZ33)

    Refining Proposal 3 (SECE):
    - S1: pzp, n1 (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: edges: both, ton: 3e-5, phase: 0
    - L1: n1, n2
    - D1: n2, out (DSCH)
    - C1: out, 0
    - D_clamp: out, 0 (DZ33)

    One detail: The `ton` for SSHI is roughly $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $ton \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25\cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    The evolution strategy will optimize `ton` and `L`, so I just need to provide a reasonable starting point.

    Let's check the `S3` overvoltage again. $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V.
    A DZ33 Zener clamp on the `out` node is the best way to handle this.

    Check the ripple: $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V.
    This is very low. $C_{out}$ needs to be large. But $T_{up} \le 0.4$ s.
    A balance must be found. The evolution strategy should handle this.

    Wait, for the Full-Bridge SSHI, the diode orientation is:
    - D1: pzp $\to$ out
    - D2: pzn $\to$ out
    - D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
    - D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
    Wait, if pzn is ground? No, the piezo is between pzp and pzn. The FBR is:
    D1: pzp $\to$ out
    D2: pzn $\to$ out
    D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
    D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
    This means when pzp is positive and pzn is negative, D1 and D4 conduct.
    When pzp is negative and pzn is positive, D2 and D3 conduct.
    This is the correct full bridge.

    Final structure check:
    Design 1 (Half-Wave SSHI): L1(pzp-n1), S1(n1-pzn), D1(pzp-out), C1(out-0), D_clamp(out-0). (5 components + G1)
    Design 2 (Full-Bridge SSHI): L1(pzp-n1), S1(n1-pzn), D1(pzp-out), D2(pzn-out), D3(0-pzp), D4(0-pzn), C1(out-0), D_clamp(out-0). (8 components + G1)
    Design 3 (SECE): S1(pzp-n1), L1(n1-n2), D1(n2-out), C1(out-0), D_clamp(out-0). (5 components + G1)

    Wait, for Design 3 (SECE), is there a better way?
    In SECE, the switch is usually in series with the piezo.
    Piezo $\to$ S $\to$ L $\to$ D $\to$ C.
    This is exactly what I wrote: pzp $\to$ S1 $\to$ n1 $\to$ L1 $\to$ n2 $\to$ D1 $\to$ out.
    Actually, SECE is very effective for low $V_{OC}$.

    Let's refine the SECE one more time. In SECE, we want to extract charge when $|V_{pzp}|$ is max.
    The switch S1 should connect pzp to the extraction circuit.
    S1: pzp to n1.
    L1: n1 to n2.
    D1: n2 to out.
    This looks correct.

    One last thing: the `S` components are limited to 4. I'm only using 1.
    The `SYNC` components are limited to 2. I'm only using 1.
    The total components are limited to 16. I'm well within that.
